prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Egg-white house, old ache in the rafters, small as a button but yearning for zero: a sparrow parts the chimney and veers for my face. I wanted my nevers again, my immaculate touch-down to the durable granite of love too heavy to move: this gift, implacable bird's-eye sorrow reared from the original fairy tale's page— I don't like it. I offered no signature, my nature altered, and I'm over my hurricane. Rocking room to room, this bird threatens my gravity, threaded through like a pearl from the evening's stem. Didn't I break all eighty-eight bones of my compass, my wingspan spun from my awkwardness? This bird returns to the shell with monstrous wings, wings clumsy as shovels in a fist of dirt. It's covered with ashes, sloughing off cloud—caught in my hair, brown tumor bulged upside down on the floor to meet the applause: this blessing's too unwieldy. But open one door, one terriblegoodbye, hello—the sparrow flings like a shout for the trees.

### Option 1: Refined Literary Prose (Recommended)
*This version smooths the rhythm and sharpens the phrasing, giving it the voice of a published essay or literary work.*

I longed for my absolute boundaries once more, an immaculate touchdown upon the enduring granite of a love too heavy to move. Instead, I am met with this gift: an implacable, bird’s-eye sorrow reared from the pages of an original fairy tale—and I do not want it. I offered no signature; my nature has altered, and I have moved beyond my storm. 
> 
> Rocking from room to room, this bird destabilizes my gravity, threaded through the air like a pearl from the evening’s stem. Did I not shatter all eighty-eight bones of my own compass, my wingspan spun entirely from my own awkwardness? Now, the bird retreats toward its shell with monstrous wings—wings as clumsy as shovels plunged into a fist of dirt. Covered in ashes and sloughing off cloud, it becomes tangled in my hair, a dark growth bulged upside down on the floor to meet its applause. This blessing is simply too unwieldy. Yet, open a single door—one terrible goodbye, one hello—and the sparrow flings itself like a shout toward the trees.

A small bird, desperate for absolute void, plummets through the hearth flue into a pale-walled home that retains a long-standing pain in its roof timber, diving straight at my eyes. 

I wished only to recover my lost absolutes—to land cleanly upon the heavy, immovable stone of a solid devotion. Instead, I am presented with this unyielding, aerial grief drawn straight from an ancient fable, and I resent it. I never signed up for this; my core has shifted, and I have already survived my own chaos. 

Fluttering from space to space, the creature disrupts my stability, threading through the rooms like a bead strung from the twilight. Did I not already shatter every single strut of my internal orientation, weaving my own broad reach out of sheer clumsiness? 

Now, the bird attempts to retreat into its unborn state, despite wielding massive, awkward wings that resemble spades digging into soil. Smearing soot and dripping mist, it tangles in my hair before landing as a twisted, brown mass upside down on the floorboards, seemingly awaiting praise. This gift is far too cumbersome to hold. 

Yet, by unlatching a single exit—a painful blend of farewell and arrival—the bird launches itself toward the forest like a sudden scream.

The silence of the house was broken without warning when a small sparrow tumbled through the flue of the chimney, bringing with it a sudden cloud of dust and soot. It was an uninvited entry, dropping straight into a space that had taken a long time to quiet down. 

My immediate reaction was one of sharp resistance. The bird felt less like a lost animal and more like an unwelcome arrival of old sorrow—a ghost I thought I had already laid to rest. I had spent considerable effort clawing my way out of previous emotional storms, laboriously rebuilding a sense of calm. I resented this sudden intrusion, unwilling to let a stray reminder of darkness pull me back into a climate of grief I believed I had outgrown.

Panic took hold of the creature almost instantly. It launched into a frantic, chaotic flight, ricocheting from room to room, striking light fixtures and swooping low against the walls. The wildness of its movement was deeply unsettling. The calm I had constructed felt fragile, and the bird's erratic trajectory threatened to undo my hard-won equilibrium, destabilizing the very air in the room.

As I watched it struggle, I saw that it was heavily dusted in grey ash from its passage through the chimney. Its flight was clumsy and desperate, weighed down by the grime of the dark chute it had just emerged from. Though physically small, the bird began to feel immense—an overwhelming, unwieldy burden thrashing against the boundaries of my living room, carrying the literal and metaphorical remnants of burnt-out fires.

Understanding that resisting the moment would only prolong the chaos, I moved quickly to the back of the house and threw the door wide open to the yard. The sparrow caught the sudden draft of outside air, pivoted mid-flight, and shot through the doorway into the open sky. Just like that, the violent commotion ceased. The room fell quiet again, the encounter over in a matter of moments, leaving only a quiet draft of wind and the subtle settling of dust.
outputs.L4:
The afternoon quiet of my living room was shattered by a dry, heavy thump inside the chimney flue. Before I could rise from my chair, a cloud of dark soot erupted into the hearth, rolling across the rug in a grey, silent wave. Out of the smoke burst a frantic, thrashing shape—a small, desperate projectile coated in ash. 

It was a sparrow, though it barely looked like a creature of the open sky. It looked like a living coal, coughing and terrified, its feathers matted with the accumulated grime of a long, dark drop. The moment it freed itself from the hearth, it launched into the air, throwing my domestic sanctuary into immediate disarray. My heart leaped into my throat as the bird beat its heavy, soot-laden wings against the white ceiling, leaving dark, jagged smudges in its wake. It rattled against the windowpanes, knocked against lampshades, and swept dangerously close to my face, painting my quiet room with the chaos of its panic. My home—a space I had carefully cultivated for order and comfort—felt suddenly invaded by an unruly, filthy energy.

Initially, I moved frantically, waving a folded towel to duck and dodge, desperate to regain control of the room. But my agitation only heightened the bird's terror. It finally landed high atop a bookshelf, panting, its tiny chest heaving beneath a thick crust of cinder. 

Seeing it there, I stopped moving. I sat down on the far side of the room and forced myself to be still. I realized that chasing the creature would only cause more damage, both to the room and to the bird itself. So, I chose to simply observe and endure. 

For nearly half an hour, we remained in a tense, shared stillness. The bird’s unwieldy, soot-stained presence felt like a physical manifestation of an unexpected crisis—an uninvited burden that had tumbled into my life out of nowhere, dirtying the clean edges of my routine. I watched its dark, frightened eyes, listening to the soft, dusty rustle of its feathers whenever it shifted. By refusing to match its panic, I allowed the sharp edge of my own emotional disruption to soften into a quiet, patient endurance.

When the room had settled into a heavy hush, I rose slowly, taking care not to make any sudden movements. I walked to the back door that opened onto the garden and pushed it wide open to the cool afternoon air. I stepped back into the shadows, clearing a direct line of sight between the perched bird and the daylight.

The sparrow tilted its ash-covered head toward the open doorway, catching the scent of the breeze. With a sudden, decisive leap, it dropped from the bookshelf and flew straight through the threshold. 

I followed it to the doorway and watched as it rose toward the high, leafy branches of the oak trees in the yard. Perched on a sunny bough, the sparrow gave a vigorous shake, releasing a faint grey cloud of dust from its wings before settling into the green foliage. 

I stood in the doorway and took a long, deep breath. The breeze washed through the room, sweeping away the scent of old ash and claustrophobia. The smudge marks remained on the walls, but the living storm was gone. In letting the sparrow go, I realized I had released more than just a trapped bird; I had relinquished the frustration and burden of an uninvited crisis. Closing the door softly, I stepped back into the quiet, ready to clean the ash and reclaim my peace.
outputs.L5:
Old man Didn lived in a quiet, timber-framed cottage at the edge of the Whispering Woods. He was a creature of habit, spending almost every late afternoon on his front porch, rhythmically **rocking** back and forth in his worn oak chair while listening to the wind rustle through the pines. 

One crisp autumn morning, while gathering firewood along the riverbank, **Didn** spotted something extraordinary nestled in a bed of damp moss. It was an unusual, speckled **egg**, nearly the size of a melon, smooth as river glass and faintly warm to the touch. Knowing the autumn frost would soon set in, he gently wrapped it in his wool scarf and carried it home, placing it safely on a woven nest near the hearth.

For three days, the mystery remained dormant. But on the fourth evening, as the fire crackled and Didn sat in his favorite spot **rocking** softly, a sharp tap echoed through the room. 

He froze, halting his chair mid-sway. 

On the table by the fire, the **egg** gave a sudden, deliberate tilt. It began **rocking** side to side, vibrating with a frantic energy from within. A tiny, spiderweb crack ruptured the speckled shell, followed by a soft, inquisitive chirp. **Didn** leaned forward, a wide smile breaking across his weathered face, ready to welcome whatever marvelous little stranger was about to tumble into the world.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem about an intrusive sparrow flying down a chimney into a house, serving as a metaphor for an unwelcome emotional healing or an unwieldy blessing.
counterfactuals.output:
It fell through the dry throat of the chimney—a velvet anvil, a brown bullet coated in cold creosote, coughing up decades of soot onto the pristine, frozen parlor. We had spent years cultivating the quiet rust of this room, carefully sealing the draft, learning the exact weight of our preserved darkness. And then the hearth sneezed. A panicked, violent pulse spilled onto the rug, dragging the whole sky down behind it.

It was not a gentle visitor. It was an unwieldy grace, a frantic bundle of hollow bones and muscle that refused to obey the geometry of our grief. It ricocheted off the brass lamp, bending the light until the corners of the room bled green. With every stroke of its soot-stained wings, it beat the air into strange, asymmetric fractions, shaking loose the yellowed wallpaper to reveal the plaster beneath, which immediately began to hum with the sound of melting ice. 

"Get out," we whispered, our mouths tasting of ash. But recovery is a brute; it does not knock, and it never wipes its feet. 

The sparrow shattered the cut-glass decanter—the one holding our oldest, most reliable tears—and in their place left a puddle of blinding, furious morning. It perched atop the grandfather clock, its tiny, terrified heart knocking against its ribs like a trapped hammer, forcing the pendulum to tick backward toward springtime. It smelled sickeningly of ozone, wet pine, and distance. It was too loud. It brought the vast, unmanageable horizon into a space we had built specifically to forget it.

When it finally shot through the narrow crack of the window, it took the quiet with it, leaving the drapes torn, the air bruised, and the carpet sprouting wild, stubborn clover where the cinders used to rest. We sat in the ruined, roaring light, furious and alive, our hands trembling as we reached out to touch the newly opened air.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.output:
The dawn broke in a quiet, salt-washed hush, breathing the damp relief of a hurricane that has passed. Clinging to the edge of the scoured bluff, an egg-white house stood miraculously unbroken, a pale porcelain pearl amid the tangled driftwood and sodden weeds. 

High above the altered shore, a bird with shovel-like wings scooped dark arcs through the lingering fog, as if digging through the heavy air for the lost contours of the coast. Inside the sunroom, where the gale had left only a cool, static calm, the shattered ivory mechanism of an ancient heirloom lay spread across the wet floorboards—the eighty-eight bones of a compass, stripped of north, waiting to point toward whatever world remained.

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a contemporary poem in prose form about grief entering a home unexpected? Make the language dense, strange, claustrophobic, and full of heavy imagery.
counterfactuals.output: It arrived without the courtesy of a draft, squeezing under the door casing like warm grease, a low, marrow-heavy mass that smelled of river mud and scorched wool. Instantly the ceiling dropped three inches; the amber bulb in the hallway curdled into a yellow oil that barely reached the floorboards. You were holding a teacup when the porcelain took on the mass of a granite cobble, dragging your wrist down until the linoleum received it with a dull, leaden slap. It did not introduce itself; it simply expanded by displacement, pushing the ambient oxygen out through the keyhole until the living room became a sealed, wet lung. Shadows did not stretch across the rug—they pooled into cold lard beneath the coffee table, calcifying against the baseboards. The front door swelled in its jamb, grain locking into grain until the entryway fused into an ironbound trunk of dead oak. When you tried to step back toward the kitchen, the air had already turned to raw dough, heavy and yeast-choked, filling your throat with the taste of rusted copper and old rain. Behind the drywall, the studs groaned under the sudden, suffocating weight of an extra room that had built itself inside the walls without a single window, settling its damp, velvet rump squarely upon your chest.

counterfactuals.prompt: Creative writing prompt: Describe the moment a wild creature invades your quiet, post-disaster life, forcing you to confront an old ache you thought you had moved past.
counterfactuals.output:
The silence following the collapse was not a void; it was a physical weight. For four years, I had curated it, polishing it like silver. I lived in a sun-bleached farmhouse on the edge of the abandoned salt marshes, where the world had simply run out of steam and stopped. No engines. No chatter. Just the steady, rhythmic ticking of the wind through the dead cedar trees. 

My life was a tight system of quiet rituals: mend the solar panels at dawn, tend the dry-bed squash at noon, boil the brackish well-water at dusk. It was safe. It kept the perimeter of my mind entirely clear of the past—clear of the crowded evacuation bridges, the sirens, and the exact warmth of my little sister’s hand slipping out of mine in the frantic dark, never to be found again. I had convinced myself that grief was an indulgence for a world with spare time, and I had buried it beneath four years of strict, cold survival.

Then, on a Tuesday afternoon, the wild broke through the kitchen glass.

It happened in an explosion of sound that made my heart slam against my ribs like a trapped bird. A deafening *CRASH*, followed by the skitter of boots on hardwood, the frantic clatter of my remaining ceramic mugs hitting the floor, and a wet, terrifying snarl.

I grabbed the heavy iron poker from the cold stove, my chest heaving. "Get out!" I hollered, my voice raspy from disuse. 

In the dim light of the hallway, I saw it. Not a dog, not a wolf, but a young mountain lion—ragged, emaciated, and terrified. Its coat was matted with pine pitch and burrs, its flank torn open by what looked like a bad encounter with rusted barbed wire. Blood, bright and unnervingly red, dripped from its hind leg onto my meticulously scrubbed floorboards. 

It didn't look majestic. It looked wretched. Its large, amber eyes were blown wide with the pure, unreasoning frenzy of a dying thing cornered by the light.

When I took a step forward, raising the poker to drive it back toward the shattered window, the beast turned and bolted down the narrow hall. It crashed sideways against the walls, seeking an escape, before throwing its weight against the door at the very end of the corridor. 

The door yielded with a crack. The cat tumbled inside, and the door swung half-shut behind it.

I froze. My breath hitched in my throat, freezing halfway down.

*Not that room.*

It was Lily’s room. I hadn't opened it since the summer I realized I was never going back to look for her. I had locked the door, stuffed a towel under the crack to keep the dust out, and treated that square footage of the house as if it had dissolved into the ether. 

Inside the room, the cat was tearing things apart—a muffled, desperate violence of claws tearing fabric, heavy furniture shifting, low, chest-vibrating growls. 

"No," I whispered. The iron poker suddenly felt useless in my trembling hands. "No, no, no."

I forced my feet forward. Each step down the dark hall felt like dragging my heels through wet concrete. My thumb grazed the dusty brass knob of the door. I pushed it open.

The afternoon sun poured through the grime-streaked window, cutting through the swirling dust. The cat was crouched in the far corner, bleeding into the braided rag rug Lily had made when she was seven. It was panting violently, its tongue hanging out, staring at me with a lethal mix of fear and exhaustion.

And there, strewn around the animal, was the frozen geography of my sister's life. 

The cat’s thrashing had knocked over the wooden bookshelf. A box of yellowing pencil drawings had spilled across the floor. On the wall above the beast hung Lily’s bright yellow rain slicker, still hooked to a wooden peg, untouched by time. The animal’s muddy, bloody paw prints were smeared across a white stuffed bear that lay torn on the rug.

The smell of the room hit me first—dust, dried lavender, and the faint, sweet scent of old paper—and then the animal introduced the sharp, metallic tang of fresh blood and wet fur. 

The past and the present collided with the force of a physical impact.

I looked at the cat. It was curled tightly around itself, its ribs heaving like small bellows, hissing weakly through bared teeth. It was so young. It had probably been driven out of the high woods by the drought, desperate for water, bleeding out, running until it ran out of world. 

It was fighting with everything it had just to draw its next breath.

I looked down at the yellow rain jacket. I remembered the day I bought it for her. I remembered how she used to jump in puddles until her socks were soaked, her laughter ringing out clear and loud, entirely uncaring of the mud. I remembered how hard she had fought to keep up with my longer stride as we ran toward the ferry docks on the last day—how she had panted, how her small chest had heaved, terrified, desperate, just like the creature bleeding in the corner.

For four years, I had told myself I was strong because I didn't cry. I had told myself that shutting the door was an act of maturity. 

Standing in the doorway, watching that wild, wounded thing wreck the shrine I had built to my own stoicism, I realized the truth. I hadn't moved past the ache. I had only locked it in a room and left it to starve.

A sob tore from my throat—a harsh, ugly sound that startled the cat into another low snarl. My knees gave out, and I sank to the doorway, the iron poker dropping from my numb fingers and clattering against the floor. 

I wept. I wept for the yellow jacket. I wept for the hand that slipped away. I wept for the endless, agonizing quiet I had built to hide my cowardice. The grief hit me in suffocating waves, hot and furious, washing away the numbness I had spent years cultivating. I squeezed my eyes shut and let it tear through me, feeling the raw, jagged edge of the old wound as if it had been carved open just seconds ago.

The cat didn't attack. It couldn't. It just watched me, its heavy breathing matching the rhythm of my broken gasps.

When the tide of tears finally receded, leaving me hollow and stinging, the quiet returned to the room. But it was a different kind of quiet. It was no longer a tomb. 

I wiped my face with the back of my sleeve. My eyes met the amber eyes of the mountain lion. 

"Okay," I rasped, my voice thick. "Okay."

Slowly, without breaking eye contact, I reached out and grabbed the edge of a heavy woolen blanket off the small twin bed. I didn't use it as a weapon. I unfolded it, keeping my movements slow, predictable. 

I moved to the window on the opposite wall—the one that looked out toward the tree line. It was stuck with age, but I threw my weight against the sash until it burst open with a groan of wood and rusty nails, letting in the cool, sharp breeze of the marsh.

Then, holding the blanket up as a shield, I stepped aside, clearing a path from the cat’s corner straight to the open window.

"Go on," I whispered softly. "Go back out there."

The cat hesitated, its ears pinned back. It sniffed the rush of fresh air coming through the open frame. It looked at me, then at the sill, gathering the absolute last dregs of its strength. 

With a awkward, limping spring, the creature launched itself up onto the sill, paused for a fraction of a second—a silhouette of frayed orange fur against the pale gray sky—and vanished into the tall grass outside.

I stood there for a long time, watching the grass sway where it had gone.

The cold wind blew through the open window, rustling the pencil drawings on the floor, lifting the sleeve of the yellow rain jacket on the wall. The dust was gone, blown away into the afternoon. 

I looked at the bloody prints on the rug, at the shattered glass in the hall, at the messy, ruined room. It was broken. It was exposed to the elements.

I didn't close the door. I walked over to the window, sat down on the floor beneath it, and let the wild air fill my lungs.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem exploring the tension between wanting to stay isolated and being forced to let go, starting with the phrase "Egg-white house".
counterfactuals.output: Egg-white house, seamless and unblinking, where I tucked my knees against my chest and learned the soft art of disappearing. Inside, the air was a thick, pale broth where no weather could reach me; I loved the curved edges, the absolute absence of doors, the way the outside world remained only a faint, muffled rumor beyond the plaster. To stay was to remain unhatched—pure, undisturbed, preserved in a cool, calcified peace. I built a sanctuary out of stillness, believing that whatever does not open can never be broken. But safety is a stagnant thing, and time is a pressure that works even through chalk. It began with a hairline fracture, a sudden, jagged line running across the ceiling like a dark vein, spilling the terrifying scent of rain and wet soil into my sterilized room. I threw my weight against the seam, pressing my palms into the break, desperate to seal the rift with my own flesh, to keep the fragile yolk of my solitude intact. How fiercely the heart fights for its own cage. Yet the crack only widened, pulled apart by the rude, insistent fingers of the wind. The shell buckled, peeling back like dry parchment to reveal the vast, unstructured sky. The cold air stung my unaccustomed lungs; the light struck like a hammer. And there, trembling on the threshold of my own ruin, I realized the sanctuary was not being destroyed, only opened—and I had no choice left but to unclench my fists, step over the shattered walls, and let the wild, uncurtained world take me in.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
